summary: Among community-dwelling older adults living alone, less frequent preintervention social contact was associated with greater reductions in loneliness during a social robot intervention. Future trials should examine whether preintervention social contact modifies the effects of social robot interventions.
title: Participant Characteristics Associated With Loneliness Reduction During a Digital Social Robot Intervention Among Older Adults Living Alone in Japan: Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Controlled Trial

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> People with intellectual disabilities experience a disproportionate burden of preventable health conditions, often linked to low levels of physical activity and poor dietary habits. Although digital health interventions hold considerable promise for addressing these challenges, many existing solutions remain difficult to use for this population due to limited accessibility. Co-design is increasingly advocated to develop digital health solutions that better align with users’ needs, yet there is limited empirical guidance for co-design processes with people with intellectual disabilities. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aimed to explore experiences of a co-design process for developing a digital intervention for health promotion for people with intellectual disabilities, from the perspectives of members of the co-design team involved in different roles across the process. <strong>Methods:</strong> A qualitative study design was used based on 5 retrospective reflection meetings conducted in southeastern Sweden following a co-design process of 17 workshops. Eight purposively selected members of the multidisciplinary co-design team, including 4 researchers, 2 user experience designers, 1 support worker, and 1 coresearcher with intellectual disability, participated in different constellations. Reflection meetings were held between February and March 2026, and transcribed data were analyzed inductively and interpreted in relation to established co-design frameworks. <strong>Results:</strong> The findings reflect the team members’ experiences of the co-design process and point to a number of factors that appeared to support participation and collaboration. These included an extensive preparatory phase focused on recruitment and relationship building, the importance of working concretely and visually already during predesign, and the role of convivial relational practices in supporting confidence, voice, and collaboration. Time demands were mainly related to the iterative and participatory nature of co-design rather than to intellectual disability per se. Ethical considerations related to compensation were also highlighted, particularly in relation to recognizing coresearchers’ contributions on equal terms. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> By examining experiences of the co-design process, this study contributes methodological insights into how digital intervention development can be made more accessible, participatory, and responsive to the needs of people with intellectual disabilities. The findings suggest that enabling meaningful co-design with people with intellectual disabilities requires flexible interpretation of existing co-design frameworks, sustained attention to relational collaboration throughout the process while recognizing the ongoing importance of collaboration with support workers, and adaptation of methods rather than a need for development of entirely new ones. Supporting a sense of collaboration and conviviality over time, alongside addressing ethical issues of compensation for coresearchers’ work, may be critical for producing digital interventions for health promotion that are both usable and inclusive. <strong>Trial Registration:</strong>
title: Co-Designing a Digital Intervention for Health Promotion for People With Intellectual Disabilities: Qualitative Study of Team Members’ Reflections

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> When chronic kidney disease progresses to end-stage kidney disease, many patients receive in-center hemodialysis. Although lifesaving, hemodialysis is associated with intradialytic hypotension. Peer mentoring and patient activation support in hemodialysis have not been well studied. <strong>Objective:</strong> This Dialysafe study combined patient education and peer mentoring to promote health behaviors supporting prevention of intradialytic hypotension. We aimed to describe recruitment, engagement, completion, and attrition; assess participants’ health goals and self-reported behavior changes; and evaluate satisfaction and recommendations for improvement. <strong>Methods:</strong> At 10 Dialysafe hemodialysis centers assigned to patient activation, all eligible English-speaking patients were invited. The intervention comprised 5 educational modules and 5 videoconference peer-mentoring sessions. Mixed methods analyses integrated electronic health record and platform data, postintervention surveys, and clinic operations committee notes. An engagement score (range 0-50) summarized intervention use. Descriptive statistics, <i>t</i> tests, chi-square tests, logistic regression, and zero-inflated Poisson regression were used to assess recruitment, completion (all 5 mentoring sessions), and engagement. Qualitative data were inductively coded and integrated through joint displays. <strong>Results:</strong> Of the 639 eligible patients, 155 (24.3%) were recruited. Recruited patients were younger than nonrecruited patients (mean 57.6, SD 13.8, vs 64.3, SD 14.7 y; <i>P</i><.001); each additional year was associated with 4% lower odds of recruitment (odds ratio [OR] 0.96, 95% CI 0.94-0.98; <i>P</i><.001). Recruitment was more likely among college graduates (OR 1.70, 95% CI 1.02-2.83; <i>P</i>=.04) and patients with sleep disorders (OR 2.27, 95% CI 1.06-4.87; <i>P</i>=.03). Attrition was concentrated before mentoring sessions began. Of recruited patients, 72 of 155 (46.5%) met with a peer mentor and 58 of 155 (37.4%) completed all 5 sessions. Completers were 1.9 years younger (56.4, SD 13.8, vs 58.3, SD 13.9 y) and had Charlson Comorbidity Index scores 0.4 points higher (3.4, SD 2.0, vs 3.0, SD 2.3) than noncompleters. The average engagement score was 18.4 of 50 (SD 20.1). Engagement was higher among men (incidence rate ratio [IRR] 1.33, 95% CI 1.22-1.45; <i>P</i><.001), Black patients (IRR 1.27, 95% CI 1.16-1.39; <i>P</i><.001), and patients with dialysis vintage <1 year (IRR 1.22, 95% CI 1.05-1.42; <i>P</i>=.01). Higher Charlson Comorbidity Index scores predicted engagement (IRR 1.04, 95% CI 1.01-1.07; <i>P</i>=.002) and completion (OR 1.37, 95% CI 1.05-1.79; <i>P</i>=.02). Of 79 patients who set goals, 64 (81%) selected communication with the care team; 22 of 54 (40.7%) survey respondents identified this as their main behavior change. Both mentees and mentors identified peer-mentoring sessions as the most valuable component. Among mentee respondents, 55 of 55 (100%) respondents rated the program good or excellent, and 53 of 54 (98.1%) respondents would recommend it. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Participants constituted a self-selecting group. Patient-clinician communication was a priority, and participants valued peer mentoring. Digital patient activation intervention strategies to increase reach are needed. <strong>Trial Registration:</strong> ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03171545; https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT03171545
title: Recruitment, Engagement, Experiences, and Self-Reported Changes in a Digital Patient Activation Intervention to Improve Hemodialysis Session Stability: Mixed Methods Study

summary: Background: Postpolypectomy surveillance intervals derived from colonoscopy findings and histopathology should be guideline-based, yet these are frequently not adhered to, contributing to under- and oversurveillance. This motivates a more structured and automated approach to improve adherence. Objective: We developed and evaluated an automated, implementable, guideline-aligned decision support tool that extracts colorectal polyp features from free-text colonoscopy and histopathology reports and produces auditable surveillance recommendations. Methods: We extracted paired colonoscopy and histopathology reports from a National Health Service (NHS) trust and designed a 4-stage prompting pipeline using open-weight large language models to separate multispecimen histopathology reports into individual containers (“pots”), align endoscopic findings with specimens, and normalize each pot into a structured schema. The surveillance intervals were then computed by a deterministic rule engine encoding guideline rules. We evaluated extraction performance on 100 procedures (215 pots), assessed surveillance recommendation performance on a same-site cohort (n=100), and performed external validation on a cohort from a second trust (n=100). A separate retrospective audit compared automated recommendations and observed routine scheduling against a clinician-derived reference based on full electronic health record review in 127 patients. Results: Key extraction fields showed end-to-end accuracy (specimen type=0.995; location=0.981; diagnosis=0.981; excision completeness=0.949), with mean report-level pot comprehensiveness of 0.968 (SD 0.112). Overall surveillance recommendation accuracy was 0.96 (95% CI 0.90-0.98) at Guy’s and St Thomas’ NHS Foundation Trust (GSTT) and 0.93 (95% CI 0.86-0.97) at Sandwell and West Birmingham NHS Trust (SWB) and showed strong class-level performance (no follow-up -score of 0.98 at GSTT and 0.97 at SWB; site check -score of 0.93 at GSTT and 0.91 at SWB; 3-year follow-up -score of 0.86 at GSTT and 0.80 at SWB; cancer alert -score of 1.00 at GSTT and 1.00 at SWB). The comparison to current clinical practice showed that the tool would improve guideline adherence primarily by reducing potential undersurveillance. Conclusions: This hybrid approach using open-weight large language models for structured extraction and guideline-encoded rules for decision-making can generate accurate, lightweight, and auditable postpolypectomy surveillance recommendations. Such a tool has the potential to improve safety netting and guideline adherence in NHS colonoscopy workflows.
title: Improving Postpolypectomy Surveillance Decisions Using an Automated Analysis of Colonoscopy and Histopathology Reports: 2-Center Validation Study

summary: Background: Personality traits are central to understanding human behavior and life outcomes, yet their assessment remains challenging due to biases and limited expressiveness in traditional self-report inventories. The emergence of large language models (LLMs) creates new opportunities to infer personality from naturalistic text, but it remains unclear whether these systems can reliably predict validated personality traits or whether their predictions primarily reflect superficial linguistic patterns. Objective: This study evaluates the ability of LLM-based methods to predict continuous Big Five personality scores (1‐5 Likert scale) from semistructured interview transcripts and compares the performance of different modeling paradigms. Methods: We analyzed semistructured interview transcripts from 518 participants, each paired with validated self-reported Big Five scores measured using the 10-item Big Five Inventory (BFI-10). We compared four paradigms: (1) zero-shot and chain-of-thought prompting with GPT-5 mini; (2) parameter-efficient fine-tuning (low-rank adaptation) applied to open-source RoBERTa-base and LLaMA-2-7B models; (3) supervised fine-tuning of GPT-4.1 mini across two independent training runs; and (4) embedding-based regression using 4 pretrained encoders (all-mpnet-base-v2, E5-large-v2, text-embedding-3-small, and text-embedding-3-large) with a multioutput ridge regression. Results: Supervised fine-tuning yielded the strongest overall performance among the evaluated approaches. In the best-performing run, correlations reached =0.718 for conscientiousness and =0.631 for agreeableness. Neuroticism showed moderate and consistent performance across the 2 fine-tuning runs, whereas extraversion was less stable across runs. Embedding-based regression, particularly with text-embedding-3-large, achieved competitive results for conscientiousness and agreeableness, although it remained below supervised fine-tuning. Prompt-based methods showed weak and inconsistent performance across traits. Openness was generally difficult to predict, although RoBERTa-base with embedding-based low-rank adaptation fine-tuning showed modest but statistically significant performance, indicating trait- and method-dependent variability. Conclusions: LLM-based approaches exhibit trait-dependent performance in predicting personality from naturalistic dialogue, with fine-tuning substantially improving correspondence with validated psychometric scores. These findings suggest that personality inference from naturalistic dialogue is feasible but depends strongly on modeling strategy, trait domain, and the availability of supervised fine-tuning with validated personality measures.
title: Personality Inference From Semistructured Interviews Using Large Language Models: Comparative Evaluation Study

summary: Background: The COVID-19 pandemic necessitated innovative approaches to health communication, particularly for non–English-speaking communities. Vietnamese Americans, who report lower rates of English proficiency, faced unique challenges accessing facts and subsequent “infodemic” of rapidly spreading information. Objective: This study aims to evaluate the feasibility and engagement patterns of a community-engaged bilingual digital campaign delivered through Google’s Display & Video 360 (DV360) platform to Vietnamese Americans in Texas, comparing performance across multiple advertising formats. Methods: We implemented a 2-phase digital campaign on (DV360): static display advertisements (Phase 1: February 15-March 31, 2022) and audiovisual content (Phase 2: May 26-June 30, 2022). With community-based organizations (CBOs), 6 static displays, 2 videos, and 2 audio advertisements were developed in English and Vietnamese using focus group review and back-translation. Advertisement placements were constrained to a Texas Vietnamese audience segment. Total budget was US $9,472.54. Performance was evaluated using impressions, click-through rate (CTR), cost metrics, cost per click (CPC), cost per thousand impressions (CPM), and cost per view (CPV), with Wilson 95% CI, and two-proportion z-tests for substantive comparisons. Results: The campaign generated 4,974,357 impressions, reaching approximately 1.4 million unique users in Phase 1, and 105,000 in Phase 2. Vietnamese-language display advertisements achieved a higher CTR than English-language advertisements (0.105% vs 0.046%; ²=480.6; <.001; risk ratio 2.29). Mobile placements outperformed desktop within each language (Vietnamese mobile 0.156% vs desktop 0.045%; English mobile 0.064% vs desktop 0.019%). Audio CTR was 1.911% in May but fell to 0.119% in June on small denominators (≈1800 impressions; 5 clicks). Impressions concentrated in expected Texas metropolitan areas (Houston 24.4%, Dallas 19.9%, Austin 7.9%). Phase 2 Google Analytics Behavior Flow showed 55.2% of language-distinguished landings were on Vietnamese pages (²=6.7; =.01). Cost efficiency was favorable (CPC US $2.35 and CPM US $1.45). Conclusions: A community-engaged bilingual digital campaign produced measurable in-language engagement among Vietnamese American audiences in Texas. Like other COVID-19 outreach campaigns directed at historically marginalized groups, researchers worked closely with CBOs, paying particular attention to messaging, language translation, and graphic representation in display, audio, and video advertisements to reach the population of interest. What differed from other campaigns was the use of DV360 allowing dissemination across multiple platforms and devices. Results are limited to engagement because direct impact on COVID-19 immunization or participation in clinical trials was not measured. Future directions can explore more clinically significant outcomes, in-language radio advertising, and harnessing AI to develop and monitor public health campaigns.
title: Digital Campaign to Promote COVID-19 Vaccination and Clinical Trial Participation Among Vietnamese Americans: Observational Engagement Study

summary: Background: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to quantify psychological constructs from natural language, yet their outputs are typically evaluated only as predictions of an external label. When that label is itself imperfect, optimizing prediction conflates label agreement with construct measurement. No study has applied a multidomain measurement-oriented evaluation to LLM-derived psychological outputs. Objective: We applied 5 psychometric evaluation domains to LLM-derived outputs to test whether measurement-oriented evaluation surfaces properties that prediction-oriented evaluation does not: extraction repeatability, convergent validity with a lexicon-based tool, ecological concurrent validity decomposed into within-person and between-person components, incremental value in a 4-arm comparison with that tool, and method-blinded expert evaluation with structured error attribution. Methods: Thirteen linguistic features were extracted by GPT-5.2 (OpenAI) from 3556 person-days of daily voice narratives collected from 279 call center workers over 15 days via ecological momentary assessment. Features were evaluated across the 5 domains, with Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count, version 22, as the lexicon-based comparator. Multimodel robustness was assessed by re-extracting all features with Google Gemini 2.5 Flash. Results: Features showed high repeatability (mean intraclass correlation coefficient=0.987), construct-dependent convergent validity (Spearman ρ=0.08 to 0.79), and within-person tracking of same-day stress (negative emotion β=0.68). In a 4-arm comparison (baseline, baseline plus lexicon features, baseline plus LLM-derived features, and baseline plus both), LLM features increased explained variance in daily stress from 13.2% to 30.4%, versus 16.9% for the lexicon-based comparator. Among transcripts sampled for maximal method discordance, experts preferred LLM-derived profiles in 83.7% (261/312) of blinded decisions. Error analysis showed that 53% (35/66) of false-positive attributions reflected reference-label limitations, not model failures. Re-extraction with Google Gemini 2.5 Flash replicated key properties (person-level =0.94). Three phenomena were visible under measurement-oriented evaluation that prediction-oriented evaluation does not typically examine: divergence between within-person and between-person effects, reference-label limitations as a dominant error source, and moderation of feature meaning by individual differences. Conclusions: Prediction metrics alone are insufficient for evaluating LLM-derived psychological measures. Measurement-oriented evaluation revealed properties, including level-dependent effects and asymmetric error attribution, that have direct implications for how LLM-based assessment studies interpret their results. For clinical use, the measure is a complement to existing screening instruments for longitudinal monitoring, not a stand-alone diagnostic.
title: Evaluating Large Language Model–Derived Outputs as Psychological Measures: A Five-Domain Psychometric Framework With Application to Daily Stress

summary: Background: Musculoskeletal (MSK) conditions account for one in seven general practice consultations in the United Kingdom. Despite national guidelines, suboptimal care remains common. Digital clinical decision support systems (CDSSs) offer a promising route to improve care quality but have not been robustly evaluated in MSK primary care. Objective: This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy, clinical effectiveness and cost-effectiveness, carbon reduction, safety, and implementation of a CDSS (CrossCover) for MSK consultations in UK general practice. Methods: We conducted a mixed methods, cluster-randomized controlled trial in 19 general practices between February and July 2024. Practices were randomized 1:1, stratified by list size. Intervention practices received training and access to the web-based CDSS for 3 months. We analyzed anonymized electronic health records to identify all adult MSK consultations. The primary outcome was the proportion of patient records containing one or more of 12 predefined non–evidence-based management options, assessed by blinded clinical review of 120 patient records (60 per arm). Reviewers assessed the complete 3-month record in both arms; in the intervention arm, suboptimal management was counted only where it occurred at a consultation in which the CDSS was used. Secondary outcomes included intention-to-treat treatment comparisons of self-management advice, prescriptions, referrals, and imaging. Clinician engagement, safety, environmental and economic modeling, and clinician experiences from semistructured interviews were evaluated. Outcome assessors were blinded; clinicians were not. Results: Among 10,182 eligible patients with MSK conditions (4268 intervention; 5914 control), the CDSS was used in 365 (8.6%) patient cases. Intention-to-treat analysis identified that the intervention increased self-management alone. Per-protocol analysis demonstrated that when used, suboptimal care arose in 3% (2/60) of CDSS-guided consultations vs 25% (15/60) of control consultations (adjusted odds ratio 12.30, 95% CI 2.52‐59.9; =.002). It also increased self-management advice and community referrals, and it reduced prescribing and fit-note use. Safety concerns were logged in 6.6% (24/365) of uses with no high-risk issues identified. Environmental modeling estimated an 18% reduction in carbon emissions and 10% annual cost savings if the intervention were scaled. Interviews (n=18) highlighted positive perceptions of the CDSS’s content and safety netting but noted challenges in integration. Conclusions: When used, the CrossCover CDSS significantly reduced suboptimal primary care MSK management. However, while safety and clinician feedback were favorable, overall engagement was limited, underscoring the need for improved digital integration, workflow alignment, and implementation support. Trial Registration: ISRCTN Registry ISRCTN38924614; https://www.isrctn.com/ISRCTN38924614
title: Improving Musculoskeletal Care Quality With a Web-Based Clinical Decision Support System in UK Primary Care: Mixed Methods Cluster-Randomized Controlled Trial

summary: Background: The growing impact of generative AI (GenAI) on medical education has given rise to many reviews discussing AI literacy, trustworthiness, potential uses, and institutional or faculty benefits. However, there has been surprisingly little review-level attention to its impact on students and learning. Objective: This scoping review examines the impact of GenAI-enabled educational interventions on undergraduate medical students. Methods: We followed the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) guidelines. An electronic search was conducted between September 22 and September 24, 2025, across Ovid (MEDLINE and Embase), PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus, with no language or date restrictions, and excluding reviews, commentaries, letters, editorials, preprints, conference papers, and study protocols. Each record was independently screened by two reviewers, who thoroughly discussed and agreed upon its final inclusion in the analysis. We used a modified version of the Kirkpatrick model as an analytical framework for the final dataset. Results: Twenty-seven studies were included. Most were published in 2025 (n=21) and in the or its sister journals (n=9). The educational interventions described included GenAI used for simulated patient experiences, knowledge or decision support, and content generation. The majority of studies fell under Kirkpatrick level 1 (n=23), focusing on initial user reactions. The studies that fell under Kirkpatrick level 2 (n=16) examined learning outcomes in terms of knowledge gain, skill acquisition, and learning attitudes. No studies were classified as Kirkpatrick level 3. Three studies demonstrated explicit theoretical grounding and therefore were classified as Kirkpatrick level 4 in our modified model. Only 13 studies spanned across levels. Numerous studies fell outside the model, including studies without student-facing interventions (119 studies) and studies focused on GenAI performance (110 studies). Although these studies were not included in the final analysis, they revealed the extent to which other topics dominate the academic conversation on GenAI in medical education. Conclusions: Our review highlights the volume of studies that prioritize tool performance over learning processes, as well as a trend toward the fragmentation of educational design elements in research evaluating GenAI-enabled educational interventions. Therefore, based on our findings, we developed the Technology-Integrated Educational Design (TIED) road map that reimagines the Kirkpatrick model as a tool to guide student-centered, theory-driven, and iterative design of technology-enabled educational interventions. By integrating preinstructional exploration, mechanism-oriented thinking, educational design, implementation, and evaluation within a single student-centered framework, the road map encourages educators and researchers to consider not only whether technology-enabled interventions work and are acceptable, but also how, for whom, and under what conditions they support meaningful learning.
title: The Forgotten Student—Generative AI Use in Medical Education and the Technology-Integrated Educational Design (TIED) Road Map: Scoping Review
